The killing referred to occurred in Grant parish, and we call the attention of our authorities to the specially dastardly nature of the crime, as it seems to have been committed in an unusually cruel and cowardly manner, demanding thorough and vigorous action on their part. We do not know what our officials have done toward locating the guilty party or parties, but this certainly is a case where justice and public sentiment requires that they shall do their full duty toward arresting the guilty.

It is an outrage and a shame to have such a deed perpetrated in any community, and the good citizens of east Grant should band themselves together to run down the cut-throat murderers who have been committing so many outrages in their midst.

charles-uppher-new-york-1900-08-27.A1:
CROWD MENACES NEGRO SHOOTER
CRIES OF "LYNCH HIM," BUT THE POLICE SAVE PRISONER FROM HARM.
Charles Uppher, a colored man, fifty-one years old, who keeps a boarding house for colored seamen at No. 42 Baxter-st. and conducts a shipping office at No. 26 Coenties Slip, last night shot and seriously wounded James J. Galvin, of No. 293 Furman-st., Brooklyn. Uppher was arrested and locked up at the Old Slip station on a charge of felonious assault, while Galvin was taken to his home.

The shooting occurred on the sidewalk in front of No. 26 Coenties Slip. According to the story told by the prisoner, he was seated on an empty keg, which had been placed on the sidewalk, in front of the saloon, which occupies the ground floor. Galvin passed by, addressed an insulting remark to him, and then struck him with his fist in the face.

A scuffle followed, and a couple of blows were exchanged, then Uppher, who was getting the worst of it, started to run upstairs to his office, which is on the second floor. Galvin followed and forced his way into the office, where he assaulted the prisoner with a knife, cutting him on both hands.

Uppher then snatched up a revolver, and after chasing Galvin downstairs fired the bullet, according to eyewitnesses, which entered Galvin's mouth, knocking out three front teeth and coming out near the nose.

A big crowd gathered, made up mainly by the rough characters hovering about the river front. At one time there were loud and angry references to the race riots and crises of "Lynch him," but the prompt arrival of policement had a wholesome effect on the crowd. Late in the evening Galvin's condition was said to have changed for the worse, and before midnight it was said he was quite low.
charles-uppher-new-york-1900-08-27.A2:
NEGRO MOBBED BY WHITE SAILORS.
He'd Shot a Boarding-House Runner After Having Been Slashed Himself.
Another race riot, with about two hundred whites to one black in this case, occurred in Coenties slip yesterday afternoon. The negro was locked up afterward in the Old slip police station on a charge of felonious assault. A white man he shot is in bed at his home in Brooklyn with a bullet wound in the mouth.

The prisoner is Charles Uppher, a sailors' boarding-house keeper of 42 Baxter street and an agent for a shipping office at 26 Coenties slip. Uppher supplies sailors for the Standard Oil Company's vessels and for those of Arthur Sewall of Bath, Me., the former Vice-Presidential candidate. He is a hustler and the white men in the business who are not so successful, according to him, are jealous of his prosperity. Among the jealous ones, he says, is James J. Galvin, an expressman and a "runner" for boarding-house keepers, who lives at 293 Furman street, Brooklyn. Galvin was passing through Coenties slip yesterday afternoon when he spied Uppher sitting on an empty beer keg in front of the saloon on the ground floor of No. 26. Galvin stopped and made some remarks to the negro. The latter answered back and the two were soon engaged in a heated argument.

Then, according to Uppher, Galvin struck him. Uppher retaliated, and in the mix-up that followed began to get the best of it. Finding himself worsted, Galvin, Uppher says, whipped out a knife and slashed him across both hands. The negro rushed in the door of No. 26 and ran up the stairs, with Galvin and his knife in hot pursuit, to his office on the second floor. There he got a revolver out of his desk drawer and pointed it at Galvin. This reversed the order of pursuit and the two rushed down the stairs, Uppher doing the chasing. When they reached the street the negro fired two shots. The first went wide, but the second brought Galvin groaning to the ground.

The row in the meantime had attracted a crowd of about 200 sailors and longshoremen, who by this time were yelling, "Kill the nigger!" Uppher placed his back against the building and held the mob at bay with his revolver till Policemen Turley and Mitchell came running to the scene. With the aid of several other police men they succeeded in getting Uppher to the police station unmolested.

Ambulance Surgeon F. re. who was summoned from the Hudson street hospital found that the bullet had entered Galvin's mouth, knocking out four teeth, and had then taken an upward course and come out through the nose. The wound is painful though not necessarily mortal. Galvin was put in a cab by some friends in the crowd, and was driven to his home in Brooklyn. Later Dr. Page called at the police station and dressed the cuts on Uppher's hands.

goode-farmville-1900-08.A1:
Goode, a young negro hardly 15 years of age, was tried in the County Court of Appomattox yesterday on the charge of attempting to criminally assault Mrs. John Torrence, a highly respected lady of that county. Mrs. Torrence's husband had gone away to thresh wheat, and early in the morning Goode, who was employed on the Torrence place, crept from his room, on the upper floor, down into Mrs. Torrence's chamber, where he found her and her children asleep on a pallet which was spread out on the floor. When the negro attempted to assault her Mrs. Torrence awoke, and on seeing the negro struck him with her fist, and then, grabbing a chair, attacked him with such a will that she put him to flight. He was immediately pursued, and had he been captured he would have been lynched.

The negro was afterward caught in Farmville. It was expected that he would receive the death penalty, and when the jury returned a verdict of 18 years in the penitentiary there was much excitement and indignation and many threats of lynching. It happened that a train was due to pass Appomet ox station in a short while after the verdict was rendered, and owing to the state of the public mind the court directed the sheriff to take the prisoner to Richmond at once, which was done. It is thought that the jury were influenced in their verdict by the fact that the negro was not quite 15 years of age and that he did not possess a very bright mind.

james-meadows-chicago-1900-08-05.A1:
The colored waiters and white cooks at the Vincinnes Hotel Chicago, had a battle royal in the kitchen last Sunday morning. It seems that the cooks of the Vincinnes have been quite abusive to the waiters for some time which culminated in a race riot. A waiter by the name of James Meadows gained the displeasure of the cooks and they undertook to beat him up, but James had friends among the waiters and when the melee was over it was seen that the colored boys had successfully bombarded the fort and had won the victory. The chef, E. Weston had a portion of his lip cut off and steward, L.H. Smith had been hit over the left eye with a large projectile which will render that optic useless for the next few months. Flying missiles severally cut Anna Zartimes, while a razor wielded by one of the waiters laid Joseph Coleman, white dishwasher, in the shade. James Meadows one of the waiters was also badly cut up. About this time the police patrol arrived and fifteen employees of the hotel was given a free ride.

The kitchen was a complete wreck and debres of broken China and glass ware was piled up in every corner of the room.

While we condem and regret occurrences like the above, we are glad to know that the colored boys won.

THROUGH TO ATLANTIC CITY.

Sleeping Cars Will Run via Pennsylvania Lines August 9th.

For the annual seashore excursion over the Pennsylvania Lines, Thursday, August 9th, through car conveniences will be provided which will enable excursionists to go through to Atlantic City without changing cars. On that date Train leaving Indianapolis at 3:05 p. m., will carry a sleeping car which will be run via Philadelphia and the Delaware River Bridge route to Atlantic City.

lee-moore-junction-city-1900-08.A1: Lee Moore, colored, was shot and killed at Junction City by Officers J. W. Marcus and O. H. Burke, while resisting arrest, and the officers were exonerated by the coroner's jury.
lee-moore-junction-city-1900-08.A2:
Killed by Officers.
Lee Moore, colored, was shot and killed by officers at Junction City. The officers had served a warrant of arrest on Moore in his yard, when Moore began cursing them and ran into the house and procured a pistol. As he started to raise the weapon to fire, a bullet from one of the officers' pistols pierced his heart and he fell dead.

EVENTS OF EVERYWHERE.
A monument to the late Senator Vance was unveiled at Raleigh, N. C.

In a freight train collision at Kenirco, N. Y., seven persons were killed.

Some one beat Miss Catherine Scharb to death with a hammer in New York.

The strike of firemen, stokers and sailors at Marseilles, France, has been settled.

The steamer St. Louis carried 128,000 ounces of silver from New York to Liverpool.

While resisting arrest, Lee Moore colored, was shot to death at Junction City, Ark.

Last year 2400 duels were fought in the Italian army, from which 480 deaths resulted.

It is estimated that the damage caused by the forest fires in Colorado and Wyoming will amount to $10,000,-000.

Somewhere between Chicago and Burlington, Ia., a package in charge of the Adams Express company is alleged to have gone estray.

The Berlin Lokal Anzeiger announces the engagement of Queen Wilhelmina to Prince Frederick Adolph of Mecklenberg-Schwerin.

A contract for four steel steamships to ply in the Atlantic and gulf coast trade was given the American Shipbuilding company by a syndicate of New York capitalists.

While in bathing at Old Orchard Me., John B. Clough, clerk of courts at Memphis, Tenn., was seriously injured by a wave. The physicians say that it is a very peculiar case.

Operations were resumed at all the factories of the National Glass company (tableware combination at Pittsburg, Pa.) The resumption gives employment to 4000 men.

George Hudgins and Ike Chandler well diggers, while digging a well at Hot Springs, Ark., were suffocated Chandler was endeavoring to rescue Hudgins.

At Philadelphia, while frightening a crowd of negroes by pretending she was a ghost, Florence Almond, aged 15 years, was struck on the head with a brick thrown by one of the negroes and killed.

A mob was formed in Warwick county, Indiana, to take James D. Kritb from the Booneville jail and lynch him. He was spirited away to Evansville. He is charged with the murder of Miss Nora Kiefer.

George Cabot Lodge, son of Senator Henry Cabot Lodge, and Miss Matilda Frelinghuysen Davis, the daughter of Judge John Davis of the court of claims, Washington, D. C., were married at the Episcopal Church of the Advent in Beston.

The entire plant of the Kelley Axe Manufacturing company, at Alexandria, Ind., valued at $800,000, was destroyed by fire. This was the largest axe factory in fire. This was the largest axe factory in the world, employing 800 or 1000 men when running at full force.

Sol Bloom, a Chicago music publisher, brought suit for $50,000 damages against the Union restaurant and hotel in Randolph street for refusing to serve him while he was clad in a shirt waist and minus a coat.

William H. Lawrence, one of the original negro minstrels and the possessor of one of the most tuneful tenor voices ever heard on the stage, died in Chicago of Bright's disease, aged 69 years.

The British consul at New York stated that he has received sixteen complaints from colored men claiming to be British subjects, who state that they were injured in the recent race rioting in New York.

lloyd-lee-new-york-1900-08-15.A1:
POLICEMAN'S DEATH A MURDER.
THORPE WAS ARRESTING A COLORED WOMAN WHEN HE WAS STABBED.
Patrolman Robert J. Thorpe, of the West Forty-seventh-st. station, who was stabbed early Sunday by Arthur Harris, colored, of No. 341 West Forty-first-st., at Eighth-ave. and Forty-first-st., died yesterday at Roosevelt Hospital as the result of the wound.

Thorpe, in plain clothes, arrested May Enoch, of No. 241 West Forty-first-st., who passes as Harris's wife, Sunday morning on a charge of loitering. She was being taken to the station when Harris ran out of the side door of a saloon and remonstrated with Thorpe. A crowd of negroes gathered. Thorpe was attacked, knocked down and beaten. He got to his feet again, grabbed the woman and struck Harris with his night stick. Harris, it is alleged, drew a knife or razor and stabbed the policeman three times in the abdomen.

Detective Duane and Policemen Flynn, Walton and Winnefield found Thorpe lying on the sidewalk nearly unconscious. May Enoch was arrested and identified by Thorpe as the woman he had arrested. Coroner Bausch remanded her to the House of Detention.

Detective Trojan, of the West Thirty-seventh-st. station, later in the day arraigned in the West Side Court Samuel Felneth, colored, thirty-seven years old, of No. 523 West Forty-fifth-st., charged with being a suspicious character. He was remanded to the station to await a further investigation. Felneth was arrested in Brooklyn by Acting Captain Cooney, of the West Thirty-seventh-st. station, who says he has evidence to the effect that Harris and Felneth were together to the effect that Harris and Felneth were together early yesterday about the time of the stabbing, and that he is certain the prisoner knows something of the affair.
lloyd-lee-new-york-1900-08-15.A2:
WEST SIDE RACE RIOT.
MOB ATTACKS NEGROES FOR POLICEMAN'S DEATH.
BATTLE SPREADS INTO BROADWAY
SCORES HURT - COLORED MEN
DRAGGED FROM STREET CARS
HUNDREDS OF POLICEMEN
FIGHT THE MOB.
FIGHT THE MOB.

A race riot of formidable proportions broke out last night on the West Side. A mob of white men, which grew with great rapidity from a few score to many hundreds, raged through the district and negroes, regardless of age or sex, were indiscriminately attacked. Scores were injured. The police reserves from the West Forty-seventh-st., West Thirtieth-st., West Thirty-seventh-st. and West Twentieth-st. stations, numbering four hundred or more men, were turned out. It took their efforts, combined with as many more policemen on regular patrol duty in the four precincts, to restor-order.

Clubs were used until the policemen were almost exhausted. Revolvers were emptied into the air, and in one or two instances fired at the upper stories of the negro tenements, from which the negroes defensively fired bricks, paving stones and other missiles. That many negroes were not killed outright is miraculous, for the mob at times was frenzied.

The trouble grew out of the death of Policeman Robert J. Thorpe, of the West Thirty-seventh-st. station, as the result of a murderous assault by a negro early on Sunday morning at Eighth-ave. and Forty-first-st. Thorpe was attempting to arrest a colored woman when Arthur Harris and another negro attacked the policeman with razors. They literally slashed the policeman into ribbons. He died the following day.

The policeman's death aroused the white residents of the district included from Twentieth-st. to Forty-second-st. and from Ninth-ave. to Sixth-ave. Open threats against the negroes were made, and the blacks replied in kind. While not condoning the offence of Harris, they insisted that he was only one man, and that the race ought not to be blamed for his action.

The policeman's body was taken to his home last night in Ninth-ave., between Thirty-sixth and Thirty-seventh sts. At once the house became a sort of shrine, and from all over the neighborhood men and women called to pay their respects. Many carried handsome floral pieces. As the night grew on the hatred of the negroes seemed to grow. The fact that many saloons roundabout were crowded had its influence, doubtless, on the rising tide of anger. A small group gathered about the policeman's home, and Captain Cooney, of the West Thirty-seventh-st. police station, sent a small squad of men. Trouble was not anticipated, however, and the squad was in the nature of a guard of honor for their dead comrade.

THE TROUBLE STARTS.

A few minutes before 11 o'clock a large Irish woman under the influence of drink came out of the place. She set up a howl and began to recite the virtues of the dead policeman. She first told of the beautiful flowers which had been sent, and then began to call down all the curses she could muster on the negroes.

"The black bastes ought to be kilt!" she shrieked. Just then a young negro, not more than seventeen years old, walked by. The white men made a rush for him, and he was quickly surrounded. He was beaten and kicked, and was rescued only with great difficulty. If there had been a carefully arranged plot and this had been the agreed signal the outbreak could not have been more spontaneous. Men and women poured by the hundred from the neighboring tenements. Negroes were set upon wherever they could be found and brutally beaten. The blacks at first offered resistance, but they were so soon outnumbered that they fled without delay.

For the next hour the streets for blocks were filled with a rioting, surging mob. It was a scene on very much the same order as took place a few days ago in New-Orleans. New-York has seldom had its equal. The shouting of the men, the shrieking of the women, the lamentations of the children, the shooting of revolvers and crashing of windows all made a perfect pandemonium.

Acting Captain Cooney at once ordered out his reserves, but his men were only half-hearted in their work. Some of them even went so far as to quietly encourage the whites in their disorderly work.

Nathan Arlington, eighteen years old, a colored youth, of No. 315 West Forty-fifth-st., rode up Eighth-ave. on his wheel and into the rioting crowd of whites. He was instantly surrounded, pulled from his wheel and brutally beaten. Some observers said that half a dozen policemen on the corner made no effort to save him. The leader of the mob was a young man in a gray suit, and could easily have been arrested. One of the white men had the temerity to ask a policeman for his club to kill the young negro.

"I'd like to give it to you," the policeman replied.

The negro in some way got to his feet and ran up on the stoop of No. 305 Eighth-ave. He was again attacked, the police looking on. Postal messenger No. 598, a husky boy, saw the negro's peril, and, fighting like a fiend, the messenger drove the crowd back and got the negro into the house. The policemen then made a show of authority and dispersed the crowd.

Captain Cooney at once called out the reserves from the adjoining precincts. The policemen in other parts did much clubbing, but the injured men were all negroes.

MUCH CLUBBING BY POLICEMEN.

Lloyd Lee, of Thirty-seventh-st. and Seventh-ave., was shot in the cheek and received a scalp wound and a broken arm near his home. He said a policeman had shot and clubbed him. He was taken to Bellevue Hospital.

John B. Mallory, eighteen years old, an intelligent young negro and a student in a civil engineering class, was going home from the Colored Engineers' Club, at Twenty-ninth-st. and Seventh-ave., with Gordon Jones, another student about his age. The gang jumped on them at Thirty-seventh-st. and Ninth-ave. Mal-
lloyd-lee-new-york-1900-08-15.A11:
Scores of Negroes Injured.
Staggering mobs gave chase to solitary negroes, pulled them from doorways, cable cars and other refuges, oat them into insensibility in most cases, and in at least one instance attempted a lynching. That the victim is alive is due to the fact that there was no good place to fasten the rope. Sixty or perhaps a hundred negroes were injured more or less severely, a dozen white men were battered up, and Detective Kennedy was carved up by a razor-wielding negro and is now in the New York hospital dangerously wounded, and two other policemen were injured. For many hours the police reserves from four stations were charging upon the rioters, and police patrol wagons and ambulances lined the thoroughfares where the thickest of the fight was on. This force became inadequate, and before midnight Chief Devery at the head of hundreds of reserves struggled to secure control of the turbulent and increasing mobs.
lloyd-lee-new-york-1900-08-15.A13:
A GREAT RIOT
IN NEW YORK.
Scenes Nearly as Bad as Those
in New Orleans.
THE POLICE WERE ACTIVE.
A Howling Mob Rushed About Seeking the Blood of Negroes - Fifty Men Were Wounded More or Less Seriously, and Forty Arrests Mado--A Number of Shots Fired - Panic Among Women-Hospital Ambulances Were Kept Busy Removing The Injured.
(By Telegraph to Virginian-Pilot.)
(By Telegraph to Virginian-Pilot.)

New York, Aug. 16.—Peace was not restored in the anti-negro riot district until after 3 o'clock this morning. During the riot it is estimated that 500 police were on duty, and ambulances from every hospital in West Side were kept busy. A police estimate of the result puts the number of wounded at fifty and the number of arrests at forty. The most determined and desperate hand-to-hand fight, which occurred during the riot, was that between Detective John Kennedy and the negro Lloyd Lee. Lee acted like a madman when Kennedy ordered him to move on. Refusing to do so, he said to-Kennedy:

"I know you. You are Thorpe's partner. I have been laying for you," and at the same time he slashed Kennedy in the shoulder, inflicting a deep wound. Kennedy pulled his revolver and fired four shots. One bullet went through Lee's jaw.

GOT A BEATING.

Policemen came running from different direction and went in search of Lee. In the search another negro, David H. Carr, got a terrible beating, and when he was taken to Bellevue it was found that he had a fractured skull, a fractured arm and a battered face. Kennedy was taken to the New York Hospital. Later he was taken to Bellevue, where he identified Lee as his assailant. When Lee saw Kennedy he hissed forth:
lloyd-lee-new-york-1900-08-15.A14:
WEDNESDAY'S RIOTERS DEALT WITH. Magistrate Cornell Consures Some Policemen Whites Acted Like Brutes. He Says.
Nineteen prisoners were arraigned in the West Side police court yesterday morning as a result of the race rioting on Wednesday night. Of the prisoners only four were white. Spencer Walters, the negro who started the trouble by threatening two women who were standing near the house where Policeman Thorpe's body lay, was fined $5. David H. Tarr, the negro charged with stabbing Policeman Kennedy, was held without bail to await the result of the policeman's injuries. John Haines, charged with shooting a revolver at a patrol wagon, was held for examination. Eight or ten other negroes were remanded, as the police had apparently little evidence against them.

When James Wilson, a negro of 260 West Fifty-third street, was arraigned on the charge of disorderly conduct he said that when he ran to some policemen at Thirty-fifth street and Eighth avenue for assistance one of them, whom he didn't know, stepped up to him and struck him on the back of the head with his club. Policeman White said that Wilson was intoxicated, but this the negro denied. He was supported in that statement by a negro named Johnson of a comedy team appearing in "A Trip to Coontown." Johnson said Wilson left the former's house perfectly sober just before being arrested.

"It's a shame," said Johnson, "that a colored man couldn't walk with safety on the street."

"I know it," said Magistrate Cornell. "The people who were responsible for most of this were a lot of loafers, poor white trash, who attacked a lot of colored people just because one bad negro had committed a crime. I'd like to see some of these people who really caused this here in court."

Wilson was then discharged. Magistrate Cornell also said that if the published accounts of the riot were true the whites had acted "like a lot of brutes," and he censured several police-men for bringing prisoners to court without any witnesses to corroborate the complaints made against those arraigned. Two of the four white prisoners were fined, John Gill of 230 West Thirty-eighth street for brandishing a revolver in the street, and Mary Wilkinson for waving a bread knife in West Thirty-ninth street. Patrick Dugan had been arrested because he was slow in closing up his saloon at 849 West Forty-third street when the police ordered him to do so. He was discharged.

Every one of the negro prisoners bore traces of having been beaten badly. Some of them accused the police of clubbing them.

In the Jefferson Market court a half dozen alleged participants in the riots were dealt with by Magistrate Hogan. Three were negroes and three white men. Two of the negroes who said that they had been clubbed by policemen were discharged. The third was put under bonds to keep the peace. The white rowdies were fined $10 each.
lloyd-lee-new-york-1900-08-15.A20:
POLICE BRUTAL TO A NEGRO
INSPECTOR THOMPSON BROWBEATS A
COMPLAINANT-APPEALS TO
BRITISH CONSUL.
Police Inspector Thompson did a great deal yesterday to confirm the belief that the police condoned, if not actually incited, the violent attacks upon negroes which disgraced this city a few days ago. Henry J. Down, a young colored man, of No. 342 West Fifty-first-st., who is a member of the committee of colored men of that neighborhood who are trying to prosecute some of the recent rioters, was at Police Headquarters yesterday to bring charges against Sergeant Morgan, of the West Thirty-seventh-st. police station. On Sunday Down went to Bellevue Hospital to try to see Lloyd Lee, who was shot by policeman Kennedy, 'n order to get him counsel. He was not allowed to enter, and was told to go to see Captain Cooney, of the West Thirty-seventh-st. station, for permission. Down waited until Monday and then went to the police station, and found that the acting captain was out. Sergeant Morgan was at the desk. Down stated his business and was treated gruffly by the sergeant, who, Down alleges, threatened to lock him up. Down dared him to do so, but the sergeant did not avail himself of the opportunity.

Down then went to Police Headquarters and made a complaint to Inspector Thompson. The inspector told him to return yesterday and he would have the sergeant there. Down went to Police Headquarters yesterday morning, in company with Harry Reed, of No. 346 West Forty-first-st., and W. H. Cooper, of No. 340 West Forty-fifth-st. Morgan was there in full uniform.

Inspector Thompson treated Down no more civilly than Morgan had done, and accused the colored man of being intoxicated. "You're too damned smart," said the inspector. "You're one of those smart niggers." Down replied: "I was told by both white men and colored men not to come here, as I would not get civil treatment. I came to see how I would be treated."

Down called the inspector "Mr. Thompson," which he resented. "Don't call me 'Mr. Thompson.' That sounds as if you were a gentleman." said the inspector.

Inspector Thompson then turned to Sergeant Morgan and said: "You had orders to issue no passes, didn't you?" Down interrupted by saying that Morgan did not tell him so. "That's none of your damned business!" broke in the inspector. Thompson then turned to Sergeant Morgan and said: "Go back to your station house and do the same over again if necessity requires." Down then left the building. He said that it was a fact that Policeman Kennedy, the man who shot Lloyd Lee, told a gang of thugs on the West Side to cause trouble with the negroes and the police would then club them. Down said that this was whispered about the negro quarter on the afternoon before the riot started.

Alfred A. Akins, of No. 125 West Twenty-seventh-st., one of the negroes beaten by the mob in the race riots of August 15, claims that he is a British subject. The British Consul is now investigating his claim. Akins, who is thirty years old, and is employed as a parlor car porter by the New-York, New-Haven and Hartford Railroad, says he is a native of Kingston, Jamaica, and therefore a subject of Great Britain.

His story of what happened to him on the night of August 15 is substantially this:

He reached the Grand Central Station from the White Mountains about 8 o'clock that evening. As he had not heard of the race riots then going on, he went home by going through Forty-second-st. to Seventh-ave, and turning south. At Forty-first-st. the mob, which was on the watch for negroes, saw him, and, shouting, "There's another black devil!" they seized him. They knocked him down, but he got up and succeeded in making his escape. He was not free long, however, for he was caught again, this time at Forty-third-st.

Their chase increased their anger, and they dragged him back to Forty-first-st. They cut his face in five or six places, and his right eye swelled up so he could not see out of it.

A policeman, who had been assured by some one near by that the negro had done no harm, took him away from his tormentors and helped him into a drug store. An ambulance was called, and when it came the physician dressed Akins's wounds. The ambulance started with him toward the police
him away from his corpse and helped him into a drug store. An ambulance was called, and when it came the physician dressed Akins's wounds. The ambulance started with him toward the police station, but it was stopped by the mob before it had gone far, and the negro was in danger again. The crowds spat on him without the police interfering.

When, at 2 o'clock, the ambulance succeeded in reaching the West Thirty-seventh-st. police station with its occupant, no charge was made against Akins. He was told, as were a number of other negroes about the station, to go home. But Akins begged to stay, as he feared the mob outside. He was permitted to remain until 4 o'clock, and then, when he was ordered to go, Acting Captain Cooney, he says, added this: "I hope the police will catch you before you get home and beat you to death."

The acting captain, however, declares that this statement "is a lie."

After being turned out of the station Akins was not molested, as the rain, which was then falling heavily, had driven his foes indoors. Since then he has been receiving treatment at the New-York Hospital. On Tuesday he went to the office of the British Consul-General, and saw C. Clive-Bayley, who, in the absence of Sir Percy Sanderson, is Acting British Consul. Akins related his experience, and Mr. Clive-Bayley told him to have his complaint put in legal form. Akins was referred to the Legal Aid Society. Later in the day, before Joseph B. Braman, notary public, of Nos. 120 and 1,274 Broadway, he signed and swore to an affidavit stating that he was a British subject, and had been molested without cause by a mob in the streets of New-York.

CORONER'S INQUEST ON ROBERT J. THORPE

Coroner Bausch and a jury held an inquest yesterday afternoon into the cause of the death of Robert J. Thorpe, the policeman of the West Thirty-seventh-st. station, who died August 13. They found that Thorpe came to his death from stab wounds inflicted by Arthur Harris, colored, now under arrest in Washington, D. C. Harris has been indicted by the Grand Jury of this county and extradition papers have been sent to Washington to have him brought back. Thorpe arrested a young woman named May Enoch on August 12 and Harris attempted to rescue her. Thorpe resisted and Harris stabbed him in the abdomen.

CHARGES A POLICEMAN WITH CLUBBING.

William Richardson, one of the leaders of the Tammany Colored Democracy, with headquarters near Seventh-ave., in West Fifty-third-st., called at Inspector Thompson's office yesterday and preferred charges against Policeman Reilly, of the West Thirty-seventh-st. station, who, he alleges, clubbed him without cause on August 15. Hearing in the case was postponed until next Monday.
lloyd-lee-new-york-1900-08-15.A22:
RACE RIOT IN NEW YORK.
Mobs of Whites Giving Chase to Negroes Are Aided by the Police.

New York—A mob of several hundred persons formed at 11 o'clock Wednesday in front of the home of Policeman Robert J. Thorpe Thirty-seventh street and Ninth avenue, to wreak vengeance upon the negroes of that neighborhood because one of their race had caused the policeman's death. Troops was stabbed and bruised Sunday night by negroes while he was attempting to arrest a colored woman, and died the following day. The man who inflicted most of the injuries is said to be Arthur Harris a negro who came here several weeks ago from Washington.

In a few moments the mob swelled to 1,500 people or more, and as they became violent the negroes fled in terror into any hiding place they could find.

Police were called and about four hundred responded, but instead of attempting to quell the riot they practically joined in and the negroes were given a race war second only to that in New Orleans a short time ago, Many of them were badly bruised, but none were killed, and no arrests have been made as a result of the riot.

First in New Orleans and then a repetition on a smaller scale of the disgraceful scenes of the southern metropolis in New York, and then the attempted lynching of a colored man in Chicago. lloyd-lee-new-york-1900-08-15.A29:
Tammany and the Negro. BY JOHN E. BRUCE.
---

Mr. Croker's organ, The New York Telegraph, seems to regard the stringing up of a Negro to a lamp post in the streets of New York by the mob during the late riots in that city as a very rich joke. The incident seems to have furnished considerable matter for its facetious space writers, who were brutally witty at the expense of this innocent and outraged Negro citizen.

The Tammany police are the real aggressors and the criminals who should be punished for that disgraceful riot. The system of highway robbery introduced into the Tenderloin and other districts of New York City by police captains and their go betweens, by which they exact blood money from the criminal classes in return for immunity from arrest for open violation of the law, is the true cause of the recent riot there and the terrible consequences which followed it.

The New York Democrats of the baser element are not novices at the business of hanging Negroes to lamp posts. They tried their hands at that business during the draft riots in 1868, which have gone into history, and they made themselves infamous by breaking into the Negro orphan asylum and murdering innocent Negro babes in other quarters of the city. Of course the Negro Democracy of New York led by Chief Lee will march the black legions to the polls in November next, and vote them solidly for Bryan and Stevenson. They would not be good and consistent Democrats if they did not lick the hands that smote them.
lloyd-lee-new-york-1900-08-15.A33:
POLICE DEFY PEOPLE.
COMMISSIONERS SEEM DETERMINED TO STAND BY THE FORCE.
MAYOR WILL DO NOTHING TO REMOVE
BLOT OF RACE RIOT FROM
THE CITY'S RECORD.
Considerable interest is felt over the disposition which the Police Commissioners may make this week of the formal charges that Frank Moss has filed with them against Chief Devery, Inspector Thompson and Acting Captain Cooney, of the Twentieth Precinct, growing out of the race riots of last month. It is generally expected that the Board will refuse to entertain them, since the Commissioners seem to have become part and parcel of the force, whose motto is, "Stick together." They will take this bold course, probably, for the alleged reason that the Commissioners are prosecuting an inquiry of their own into the conduct of the police at the recent riots with the avowed intention of finding out if charges ought to be brought against any member of the force. If they find no reason for bringing any charge they will certainly not entertain Mr. Moss's, it is said.

But the manner in which this investigation was begun last week clearly shows that it is scheduled to end in a "whitewash" for all those policemen who clubbed negroes in the riot or instigated others to beat them.

Frank Moss, who has been retained by the Citizen's Protective League to bring the clubbers to justice if possible, was asked yesterday what the prospects of success were, and he replied as follows:

My clients are not bringing any suits against the city for personal damages. They merely want to be assured that they will be protected in their rights in future, and for that purpose the responsibility of the police for instigating and permitting the riots of last month should be fixed where it belongs. I have gathered evidence of the clubbing of peaceable negroes in thirty distinct and different cases. In nearly all of these the negroes were caught singly by the clubbers, and each as he was clubbed was in the centre of a group of rioters packed closely around him, so that nearly all the witnesses were against him. Naturally, they will contradict flatly the negro's story that he was clubbed at all. This will make it extremely difficult to secure evidence enough to cause District Attorney Gardiner to ask a Grand Jury for indictment against any individual patrolman, and even if a few indictments should be found against patrolmen, they could easily be held back from prosecution for an indefinite period, if the District Attorney so wished.

Witnesses, too, are exceedingly timid about testifying against the police, several white men having begged me not to subpoena them, saying: "Mr. Moss, if we were to tell truthfully what we saw in those riots the police would allow bands of young ruffians to smash our windows and beat our children in the streets with impunity. We would suffer in innumerable small ways. Do not subpoena us, for we dare not testify against the police."

For these and similar reasons the outlook for bringing any patrolman to justice is not bright, but if a body of United States troops had been sent to this city to do riot duty and the soldiers, instead of suppressing the disorder, had fomented and taken part in it, what do you think would be the fate of their officers? Would they not be cashiered as incompetent and inefficient? Of course they would. Therefore I say that Chief Devery, at the head of the force; Inspector Thompson, in whose district the riots occurred, and Acting Captain Cooney, in whose precinct they raged most violently, are fairly open to charges of incompetency and inefficiency to control their men. If the charge of inefficiency be sustained it is, by the police regulations, sufficient cause for removal. Now let us see where the responsibility belongs for this blot upon the city's record. These riots began on August 15, nearly a month ago. How many clubbers have been put on trial yet? Not one. One would have supposed that the Chief of Police would have filed a complaint against some one before a month had passed. Has he? No. Then surely the Police Commissioners must have called upon the Captain of the riot precinct to explain? No. Then without doubt the Mayor must have taken some step to remove this stigma from the metropolis of the country? Not a step. Perhaps he intended to, but forgot it? No such charitable theory can be entertained.

mary-coleman-helena-1900-08.A1:
Shot by a Policeman.
Mary Coleman, colored, was shot and mortally wounded by a policeman at Helena. In attempting to arrest the woman she got hold of the officer's pistol. He borrowed another and pursued the woman, and when within a few feet of her she began firing at him. He returned the fire, and the woman fell with three bullets in her abdomen.

spencer-hampton-1900-07-31.A1:
HAMPTON.
PAVING KING STREET-A SHOOTING
ING SCRAPE.
(Special to Virginian-Pilot.)

Hampton, Va., July 31.—Work was begun yesterday in earnest on paving King street, and unless something occurs to check it, it is likely that by to-morrow night the street will be covered with asphalt blocks.

The case of Wm. H. Pulley, charged with shooting John DeHart, resulted in a hung jury in the County Court. Both men are prominent farmers. A negro named Spencer was an important witness. He produced an anonymous letter which warned him if he testified against Pulley, he (Spencer) would be lynched. Spencer testified and said Pulley had offered him $8 to leave the State. The letter was not allowed as evidence. At last accounts Spencer had not been lynched. The case will now come to trial at the next term.

CAUSEY-JACKSON MARRIAGE.

Miss Jackson has issued cards announcing the marriage of her sister, Miss Willis Jackson to Mr. Francis Frederick Causey, on Wednesday, August 11 at St. Martins-in-the Fields, London, England. They will be at home after September 1, at Hampton.

WILL SEND GOLF TEAM. The Hampton Roads Golf Culb. which is made up largely of the lovers of the popular game in this city. will soon send a crack team of eight players to Richmond to meet the golf club of that city. The team will be selected shortly.

will-jones-newton-1900-08-26.A1:
NEWTON NEGRO THIEF SHOT.
Newton, Kas., Aug. 26.—A negro, giving his name as Will Jones, was shot by the city marshal about 7 o'clock tonight. He stole a watch from a prominent citizen, and when accused of the crime began to run. The marshal commanded him to stop, and, upon his refusal to do so, shot him in the leg. The negro admitted his guilt.,

CURRENT KANSAS FACTS.
BRIEF MENTION OF INTERESTING EVENTS OF THE WEEK.
KANSAS ITEMS OF INTEREST.
The new city building in Topeka is to be completed September 15.

The two water and light companies of Parsons have consolidated.

The state bank of Belleville has opened for business. It is a new bank.

Ralph Ingalls, the son who most resembles his father, is with the army in Manila.

Old settlers of Rooks, Norton, Graham and Phillips counties will hold a reunion at Logan, September 5 to 7.

Leavenworth coal miners threaten a strike on September 1 if their pay is not raised. About 900 men are affected.

Lawrence Boyington, assistant coach at Cornell university, is to coach the Kansas University football team this fall.

The work being done by the Santa Fe in straightening its tracks and reducing its grades is going on upon a large scale.

There is an increasing demand for contracts for Kansas hay. The crop is short from the Mississippi to the Atlantic.

Judge Otis, of Atchison, estimates Senator Ingalls' wealth at $250,000. It is said that he left his estate to Mrs. Ingalls.

Automobile races will be a part of the entertainment prepared for the good roads congress in Topeka on September 25.

Governor Stanley has appointed J. D. S. Riggs, president of Ottawa University, as a member of the state board of education.

W. J. Turner, one of the marines killed in Pekin, was a Topeka boy. During the Spanish war he served on the Indiana.

Ray Simpson, a 10-year-old boy, is plowing the wheat stubble on the home farm for another crop. He has no assistance.

A Mulvane man who deeded his property to his children, is said to have appealed to the courts for aid in obtaining food.

The boring for gas at Burlington has reached its third effort. Two deep holes were bored and one more attempt is to be made.

Dickinson county and vicinity has experienced two weeks of 100 degree weather with hot winds. Pastures and corn are cooked.

Civil service examinations are appointed at Parsons October 10; Wichita October 1 and 23; Topeka September 28; Salina October 10 and 23.

A company of volunteers is being raised in Leavenworth to go to the Orient. They offer to go as United States or Kansas volunteers.

William Jones, a negro who confessed stealing a watch, was chased by the city marshal of Newton, and, refusing to stop on the marshal's command, was shot in the leg.

A Hutchinson dispatch says that I. P. Campbell and Claude Duval have joined in asking that a new convention be held in the Seventh district to name a candidate for congress.

The First congressional district has 213,839 population; a net gain of 5,148.
The Second 227,292; net gain 2,308.
The Third 227,582, gain 9,496; the Fourth 183,688, gain 3,403; the Fifth 171,853, gain 4,807; the Sixth 168,424, gain 11,232; the Seventh 252,030, gain 17,845.

Mrs. Helen Lampkin, of Chillicothe, Mo., and her husband, both under 20 years old, were traveling towards Nebraska in a wagon, when she was attacked with typhoid fever and died at Abilene. They were very poor.

Of course it was a Kansas soldier who scaled the wall of Pekin, took up the end of the rope and his comrades climbed the rope. He enlisted in Wichita April 15, 1899. He first enlisted in Vermont in 1898. His name is Calvin S. Titus, and while in Wichita belonged to the Salvation army.

W. E. Hart, president of the National Association of Accountants, is organizing Kansas bookkeepers. The object is technical education, the exchange of ideas and the maintenance of an employment bureau.

Congressman Bowersock, of Lawrence owned the mill at Galena which was swallowed by the earth on the South Side mining ground. A large force was at work, but the men were warned by the cracking noise in the earth beneath them and escaped. The mill alone cost $8,000.

Charles Plummer, aged 14, who had just finished a term at the reform school, was killed in Wichita while trying to jump on a moving freight train.

Thomas Banks, of Arkansas City, will contest the will of Moses M. Davis of Rome, N. Y., who gave in his will $10,000 to $12,000 of his property to the Christian Scientists.
